description: Persephone Board — recommended third-party components and their Persephone skins. Each skin is written against the --p-* theme contract and is NOT bundled in the installer; an agent fetches the files it needs into the board folder as a frozen local copy. See README.md.
baseUrlNote: Resolve every skin's `skin.file` as `baseUrl + file` to fetch it on a clean machine (skins are not bundled in the installer). Pinned to `main` (not a tag): skins are version-stamped in their headers and skin drift is expected — see README.md. The manifest itself is fetchable at `baseUrl + manifest.json`.

components.name: av-grid
components.purpose: Data grid — THE DEFAULT GRID FOR A BOARD. Sortable / filterable columns (checklist funnels + a removable-chip filter bar), built-in text filters with per-column operator lists (contains, equals, startsWith, blank, notBlank), free-text search with in-cell highlighting, Excel-style range select + clipboard copy/paste, virtualized rendering, in-cell editing with validation, add/delete rows and columns, a context menu, column resize + drag-reorder, host-owned filtering/sorting, a flat-row tree gutter, leading/trailing sticky data columns, and status columns (row numbers, checkboxes) pinned left.
components.docsNote: One file, complete, written FOR AN AGENT — fetch it before building a grid board. It has a 'Driving the grid from an agent' section covering the MCP browser tools (the grid resolves gestures on `pointerdown`, which `browser_click` does not send; prefer the grid API, and see the DOM contract for selectors).
components.versionNote: Unlike the third-party entries, av-grid is NOT pinned — the vendor URLs below resolve to the newest published version, and `docs` always serves the matching api.md. It is a first-party library that moves with Persephone, so the latest release is the tested one; check `AVGrid.version` (or lib/VERSION.txt in your board) to record what you actually vendored. Last verified here: 2.11.2 (2026-09).
components.preferThisOne: Choose av-grid over Tabulator unless you need a feature it lacks. It is a port of Persephone's own internal grid (VAGrid), so it is native to the app: it reads the --p-* contract directly with NO skin to fetch and NO JS re-theming, it matches the look and keyboard behaviour of Persephone's built-in grid editors, and it renders more smoothly than Tabulator — noticeably so even on small datasets. Its built-in text filters offer per-column operator lists including contains, equals, startsWith, blank, and notBlank; hosts can own filtering and sorting; `treeColumn` supplies a gutter over flat rows; and `pinned: "left"` / `"right"` provides leading/trailing sticky data columns. Reach for Tabulator ONLY when the board genuinely needs one of: variable row heights (av-grid's `rowHeight` is uniform, explicitly), row grouping with collapsible group headers, a true tree-data engine or nested rows, three-or-more-level nested column headers (av-grid's `Column.group` supplies one group band), pagination or server-side paging, remote data transport/fetching, footer column calculations / totals, built-in export (CSV / XLSX / PDF / print), drag-to-reorder ROWS (av-grid drag-reorders columns, not rows), responsive column collapse, undo/redo history, arbitrary or interleaved data-column freezing (av-grid pins leading/trailing runs), or Tabulator's library of ready-made formatters (progress bar, star rating, traffic light) — av-grid gives you `render` / `formatValue` hooks and you write the cell yourself.

vendor.note: Download BOTH INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/) and reference them with relative paths — the board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script>/<link> will not load. RENAME the UMD bundle from .cjs to .js (e.g. lib/av-grid.umd.js) so it loads as a plain classic script; it puts the module namespace on `window.AVGrid`, and the class is `AVGrid.AVGrid` (the helpers — inferColumns, RenderGrid, Popover, … — hang off the same object). Load <script> order: lib/av-grid.umd.js → app.js.

skin.loadOrder: board-base.css → lib/av-grid.css → your board's own <style> (last, so board rules win) — and pass `injectStyles: false` to create(), or the grid appends its stylesheet AFTER your page and out-orders your overrides.
skin.cssVsJs: NO SKIN TO FETCH — this is the point of av-grid on a board. In av-grid 2.11.2, the tree gutter and text-filter controls inherit the existing --avg-* tokens and their --p-* fallbacks; no new theme token or JS re-theming is needed. Every --avg-* token falls back to its --p-* counterpart (--avg-bg→--p-bg, --avg-header-bg→--p-bg-dark, --avg-grid-line→--p-border-light, --avg-accent→--p-accent, --avg-font-size→--p-font-base, …), so the grid is themed on arrival and a live theme switch re-tints it with ZERO JavaScript and zero repaints — there is nothing to re-apply in onThemeChange. To make ONE grid deviate, set --avg-* on the grid ROOT (`grid.element.style.setProperty(...)`, or a `[data-type="render-grid"].avg-grid { … }` rule — two classes' worth of specificity); --avg-* on an ancestor does NOTHING, because the root, popovers, the virtual list and the filter bar each define the whole block on themselves. Board CSS that overrides grid chrome must likewise out-specify av-grid's own one-class selectors (write `.avg-data-cell.my-class`, not a bare `.my-class`). Two gotchas that cost real time: the grid host MUST have a definite height (`getState().viewport.width === 0` means it doesn't, and the grid renders blank), and with `filterBar: true` the grid wraps itself in `.avg-grid-wrap` — give that `height: 100%`.

components.name: Tabulator
components.purpose: Data grid — the FALLBACK grid, for the features av-grid does not have: variable row heights, row grouping, a true tree-data engine or nested rows, three-or-more-level nested column headers, pagination or server-side paging, remote data transport, footer calculations, built-in export, row drag-reorder, responsive collapse, undo history, arbitrary or interleaved data-column freezing, and a library of ready-made formatters. For a plain sortable / filterable / editable grid, prefer `av-grid` (above) — it is native to Persephone, needs no skin, and renders more smoothly.

vendor.note: Download these INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/) and reference them with relative paths — the board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script>/<link> will not load.

skin.cssVsJs: The skin styles ALL grid chrome (frame, header, rows/cells, range selection, footer/pagination, header-filter inputs, in-cell editors, menus/popups, group/calc rows, tree toggles, resize guides, alerts, toggles) via the --p-* contract, so the grid follows the app theme live. Per-value colors that Tabulator sets INLINE from JS cannot be reached from CSS — the `progress` formatter bar fill + legend, and the `traffic-light` / `color` / `star` formatters. Pass those from the live palette (`persephone.getTheme()` or the `onThemeChange` argument) in your board JS and re-apply them in `persephone.onThemeChange` (see the demo board's app.js).

components.name: Chart.js
components.purpose: Charts & plots — line, bar, doughnut/pie, radar, scatter, area, mixed. Canvas-rendered, animated, responsive; good default for dashboards.

vendor.note: Chart.js ships NO stylesheet — it draws to <canvas>, so there is nothing to @import and no CSS skin. Download the UMD bundle INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/chart.umd.js) and reference it relatively; it exposes a global `Chart`. The board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script> will not load.

skin.loadOrder: lib/chart.umd.js → chart-theme.js → app.js (no component CSS; chart-theme.js is a JS adapter, not a stylesheet)
skin.cssVsJs: Chart.js is fully JS-colored — there is no CSS skin. `chart-theme.js` exposes `window.PersephoneChartTheme` (`applyDefaults(Chart, theme)`, `palette(theme)`, `paletteN(theme, n)`, `alpha`, `mix`). Pass it a --p-* palette: at init use `persephone.theme`; on a theme switch use the palette delivered to `persephone.onThemeChange` (or `persephone.getTheme()`) — NOT a cached `persephone.theme`, which is a load snapshot and goes stale after a switch. `applyDefaults` sets Chart.defaults.color (ticks/legend/point-labels) and Chart.defaults.borderColor (grid/angle lines), so scales follow the theme with no per-chart work; dataset colors come from `palette()`. The board chrome around the canvases is styled with --p-* in index.html as usual. See the demo board's app.js for the build + onThemeChange wiring.

components.name: Flatpickr
components.purpose: Date / time picker — single date, date + time (12/24h), time-only, date range, inline calendar, week numbers, month-dropdown nav, and min/max + disabled-date constraints. Lightweight, dependency-free.

vendor.note: Download BOTH INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/) and reference them with relative paths — the board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script>/<link> will not load. The vendored CSS is the base/light theme (no theme-name suffix); that is the one the skin overrides — do NOT also vendor flatpickr's dark.css/material themes.

skin.cssVsJs: Flatpickr is fully CSS-styleable — there is NO JS-colored surface, so the whole component themes from this one stylesheet and a theme switch re-tints it with no JS (the calendar is appended to <body>, under the same <html> that carries the --p-* inline vars). The skin restyles the calendar container (incl. its pointer-arrow ::before/::after triangles + box-shadow border ring), month nav + year/month <select> spinners, weekday header, every day-cell state (hover, today=accent outline, selected/range endpoints=solid accent, in-range=accent tint via color-mix, disabled, prev/next-month, week numbers), and the time picker — all from --p-*. Flatpickr's three hardcoded accents (#569ff7 selection, #959ea9 today, #f64747 arrow-hover) are replaced with --p-accent. NOTE: flatpickr does NOT style the text <input> itself — the board owns that; style your input with --p-* in your own CSS (see the demo board).

components.name: Tom Select
components.purpose: Rich select / tags / autocomplete — searchable single + multi select, removable tag chips, create-on-the-fly values, option groups, remote/async options, and keyboard navigation. Dependency-free.

vendor.note: Download BOTH INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/) and reference them with relative paths — the board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script>/<link> will not load. Vendor tom-select.css (the default theme — the one the skin overrides) and tom-select.complete.min.js (the build that bundles all plugins: remove_button, dropdown_input, clear_button, etc.). Do NOT also vendor the bootstrap5/material theme CSS.

skin.cssVsJs: Tom Select is fully CSS-styleable — there is NO JS-colored surface, so the whole component themes from this one stylesheet and a theme switch re-tints it with no JS (the dropdown is rendered under the same <html> that carries the --p-* inline vars). The skin restyles the control box (mirrors the board's inputs: --p-bg + --p-border, accent focus ring), the text input + placeholder, selected-item/tag chips (neutral tint + accent on .active) with the remove_button, the dropdown panel + box-shadow, optgroup headers, options (the keyboard/hover .active row = solid accent, like the app's menus), the matched-substring .highlight, the loading spinner, and the dropdown_input/dropdown_header plugins — all from --p-*. Tom Select's hardcoded accents (#f5fafd/#495c68 active option, rgba(125,168,208,0.2) match highlight) are replaced with --p-accent. The control already matches the board's own inputs, so a <select>/<input> upgraded by Tom Select sits flush with the form.

components.name: marked + highlight.js
components.purpose: Markdown rendering + code highlighting — marked parses Markdown (GFM: tables, task lists, strikethrough) to HTML; highlight.js tokenizes fenced code blocks. Together they render README-style documents, release notes, AI/agent output, and code snippets.

vendor.note: TWO libraries — download BOTH JS bundles INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/) and reference them relatively; the board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script> will not load. marked.min.js exposes a global `marked` (use the bare `marked.min.js` UMD path — marked 16+ dropped the bundled UMD artifact, so that path serves the last UMD build, v15.0.12); highlight.min.js (the @highlightjs/cdn-assets 'common languages' bundle) exposes a global `hljs`. Do NOT vendor a highlight.js theme CSS — markdown.css IS the theme (highlight.js ships only class names; its colors live entirely in a theme stylesheet). marked emits no CSS of its own either.

skin.loadOrder: board-base.css → markdown.css (no component CSS to load between them — neither library ships a usable stylesheet)
skin.cssVsJs: Both halves are pure CSS skins — there is NO JS-colored surface, so a theme switch re-tints the rendered document AND the syntax colors with no JS re-render. markdown.css is ONE file with two parts: (1) rendered-markdown typography for a `.markdown-body` container — headings (h1/h2 ruled with --p-border), proportional system-font prose, lists + GFM task-list checkboxes (accent-color), blockquotes (accent left-border), GFM tables (--p-panel header, faint zebra stripes), inline code (--p-text tint pill), and the <pre> code frame (--p-panel + --p-border); (2) a highlight.js token theme mapping every .hljs-* class onto --p-* by role — keywords/tags/literals → --p-accent, titles/functions/types/built-ins/attr (e.g. JSON keys) → --p-link, strings/regexp/additions → --p-success, numbers/symbols/meta → --p-warning, comments → --p-text-muted (italic), deletions → --p-error, plain/operators/punctuation → --p-text. --p-* has no syntax palette, so the ~8 token hues fold onto the semantic colors; each is one the theme system already keeps legible on its own background (verified in both themes — the amber --p-warning is a dark amber in light themes, not an invisible yellow). Wrap marked's output in a `.markdown-body` element, then call hljs.highlightElement on each `pre code` (marked emits language-* classes that highlight.js reads).

components.name: Mermaid
components.purpose: Diagrams from text — flowcharts, sequence, class, state, ER, pie, gantt, gitgraph, and more. Renders Markdown-fenced diagram syntax to SVG; good for docs, architecture sketches, and process/state visualizations.

vendor.note: Mermaid draws SVG colored from JS — it ships NO stylesheet, so there is nothing to @import and no CSS skin. Download the bundle INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/mermaid.min.js, ~3.2 MB) and reference it relatively; it exposes a global `mermaid`. The board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script> will not load. v11 uses the async API: `mermaid.initialize(config)` (sync, call once) then `const { svg } = await mermaid.render(uniqueId, diagramText)`.

skin.loadOrder: lib/mermaid.min.js → mermaid-theme.js → app.js (no component CSS; mermaid-theme.js is a JS adapter, not a stylesheet)
skin.cssVsJs: Mermaid is fully JS-colored — there is no CSS skin. `mermaid-theme.js` exposes `window.PersephoneMermaidTheme` (`config(theme)`, `themeVariables(theme)`, `palette(theme)`, `mix`, `alpha`). `config()` returns a Mermaid init config using the customizable `theme: 'base'` with a full `themeVariables` map built from the --p-* palette — node fill/border/text (primaryColor/mainBkg=--p-panel, nodeBorder=--p-border, text=--p-text), edges (lineColor=--p-text-muted), clusters, edge labels, the complete sequence-diagram set (actors, signals, notes=--p-warning tint, activation bars=--p-accent), state labels, pie slices (pie1..12 from the palette: --p-accent, --p-success, --p-warning, --p-error, --p-link, --p-text-muted), and the gantt set (task/active/done bars, sections, grid, today line). IMPORTANT — Mermaid is NOT a live-update library: it bakes colors into the SVG at render time, so a theme switch must RE-INITIALIZE and RE-RENDER every diagram from its source (NOT just re-init — and NOT a no-op like a pure CSS skin). Take the palette from the onThemeChange argument (or getTheme()), call `mermaid.initialize(T.config(theme))`, then re-run `mermaid.render(...)` for each diagram. See the demo board's app.js for the load + re-render-on-switch wiring.

components.name: Split.js
components.purpose: Resizable layout panes — drag a gutter to resize adjacent panes; horizontal (columns) and vertical (rows) splits, nestable for IDE-style layouts (sidebar | editor / console). Tiny, dependency-free; sets only inline sizes and inserts bare gutter <div>s.

vendor.note: Split.js ships NO stylesheet — it only sets inline width/height on the panes and inserts bare `.gutter` <div>s; the gutter appearance is the author's job (that is what the skin provides). Download the UMD bundle INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/split.min.js, ~6.8 KB) and reference it relatively; it exposes a global `Split`. The board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script> will not load. API: `Split(['#a', '#b'], { sizes, minSize, gutterSize, direction })`; splits nest (use one Split per axis).

skin.loadOrder: board-base.css → split.css (no component CSS to load between them — Split.js has no stylesheet)
skin.cssVsJs: Split.js has no JS-colored surface, so this is a pure CSS skin — a theme switch re-tints the gutters with NO JS (they live under the same <html> that carries the --p-* inline vars). The skin styles the divider gutters Split.js inserts: the bar fill (--p-panel), a hover/drag tint (color-mix toward --p-accent, carried through the drag via :hover since Split.js adds no dragging class), the correct resize cursors per direction (.gutter-horizontal → col-resize, .gutter-vertical → row-resize), and a centered grip of dots drawn with a radial-gradient in --p-text-muted (brightening to --p-accent on hover) — NOT a fixed-grey PNG like Split.js's docs suggest, so the grip follows the theme. The board owns the *panes'* own look (bg/border/padding) and the *layout* (flex/float + `.gutter { flex: 0 0 auto }` so the fixed-size gutter does not shrink) in its own CSS — the skin is appearance-only. Gutters are plain non-focusable <div>s (no outline blind spot); the skin still ships a defensive `:focus-visible` accent ring (a no-op) in case a board makes a gutter keyboard-operable.

components.name: SortableJS
components.purpose: Drag-to-reorder lists & kanban — reorder items within a list and drag across lists (shared groups), with drag handles, touch/fallback support, and reorder events. Tiny, dependency-free; reorders the board's own elements.

vendor.note: SortableJS ships NO stylesheet and renders NO chrome of its own — it adopts the board's existing elements and only ADDS state classes during a drag; the skin themes those states. Download the UMD bundle INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/Sortable.min.js, ~45 KB) and reference it relatively; it exposes a global `Sortable`. The board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script> will not load. API: `new Sortable(listEl, { group, handle, animation, onEnd, … })`; a shared `group` name across lists enables cross-list drag.

skin.loadOrder: board-base.css → your own item styles → sortablejs.css (link the skin LAST — see cssVsJs)
skin.cssVsJs: SortableJS has no JS-colored surface, so this is a chrome-light pure CSS skin (same shape as Split.js) — a theme switch re-tints the states with NO JS. SortableJS renders no DOM of its own; it only ADDS state classes to YOUR elements during a drag, so the skin themes only those transient states: .sortable-ghost (drop placeholder → color-mix(--p-accent 16%, --p-bg) fill under a dashed --p-accent outline), .sortable-chosen (picked item → --p-accent ring via box-shadow), .sortable-drag + .sortable-fallback (the dragging item / floating clone → --p-panel fill, --p-accent border, --p-shadow elevation, grabbing cursor), and a convention .drag-handle (grab cursor, --p-text-muted → --p-text on hover). CRITICAL load order: link this skin AFTER your own item CSS — the state classes land on YOUR elements, so a state rule (e.g. .sortable-ghost) and your .card rule have EQUAL specificity and later-loaded wins; keep item selectors low-specificity (e.g. `.card`). The board owns item appearance + layout; the skin is drag-state appearance only. The default class names assume the default options — re-point the selectors if you set ghostClass/chosenClass/dragClass/fallbackClass. NOTE: .sortable-drag/.sortable-fallback are reliably themeable in forceFallback mode (a DOM clone follows the pointer); the demo enables it.

components.name: Tippy.js
components.purpose: Tooltips, popovers and in-board menus — hover tooltips (all placements, rich HTML), click-to-toggle interactive popovers, and dropdown/context menus. Built on Popper v2 for positioning (flip/shift, arrow).

vendor.note: THREE files — download ALL of them INTO the board folder (e.g. lib/) and reference them with relative paths; the board CSP forbids remote network, so a CDN <script>/<link> will not load. IMPORTANT: despite the `-bundle` name, jsDelivr's tippy-bundle.umd.min.js (6.3.7, ~25 KB) does NOT inline Popper — its UMD reads window.Popper, so you MUST vendor @popperjs/core (popper.min.js, exposes global `Popper`, ~20 KB) and load it BEFORE the tippy bundle, or `window.tippy` is never defined. The board webview is a clean sandbox (no nodeIntegration leak), so the UMD takes the browser-global branch and needs the real global. Tippy's CORE CSS (tippy.css, ~1.4 KB) is REQUIRED — it carries the box/arrow geometry + show/hide transforms (not just default styling); the skin only re-colors. Stick to the default `fade` animation (in core CSS) — fancier animations need extra animations/*.css files. Load <script> order: popper.min.js → tippy-bundle.umd.min.js → app.js.

skin.cssVsJs: Pure CSS skin — the bubble is appended to <body> under the same <html> that carries the --p-* inline vars, so a theme switch re-tints it with NO JS. Themed via a NAMED Tippy theme (NOT a global .tippy-box override): set `theme: 'persephone'` on each instance, and the skin targets `.tippy-box[data-theme~='persephone']`. This keeps the default look intact for any un-themed tippy and is opt-in per instance. The skin themes the BOX (chrome): --p-panel fill + a REAL --p-border (essential in light themes, where a --p-panel bubble sits on a near-white --p-bg and would otherwise have no edge), --p-text color, --p-radius-md, --p-shadow, --p-font-sm, and content padding from the spacing tokens. The arrow is a two-layer triangle (same technique as Tippy's own light-border theme): ::before front face = --p-panel (set once via the arrow's `color`, which core reads as currentColor for all placements), and ::after = a --p-border ring behind it, offset per placement so the box's 1px border continues onto the arrow. CSS-vs-CONTENT split: the skin themes only the box. An INTERACTIVE popover's CONTENT is board-owned HTML (e.g. a dropdown menu's rows, a details card) — theme that with --p-* in your OWN board CSS, like the app's menus (accent hover rows). The default theme name + arrow offsets assume the default 16px arrow; re-point selectors if you rename the theme.

components.name: Native <dialog> modal
components.purpose: Modal / dialog pattern — info modals, confirm dialogs, and form modals. NO third-party library: the native <dialog> element + dialog.showModal() provides the top-layer modal, focus trapping, ESC-to-close (the `cancel` event), and method="dialog" forms whose button value becomes returnValue. This is a pattern + skin, not a vendored component.

vendor.note: NO library to download — <dialog> is a native HTML element, fully supported by the board webview's Chromium (showModal, ::backdrop, the `cancel` event, method="dialog" + returnValue). There is no JS/CSS to vendor; only the skin (dialog.css) is fetched. Backdrop click-to-close is the one behavior the native element does NOT provide — add a few lines of board JS (compare the click point to the dialog's content rect); see the demo board's app.js.

skin.loadOrder: board-base.css → dialog.css (no component CSS to load between them — there is no library)
skin.cssVsJs: Pure CSS skin — the modal lives under the same <html> that carries the --p-* inline vars, so a theme switch re-tints it AND its backdrop with NO JS. The skin styles the panel (--p-panel fill + a REAL --p-border, essential in light themes; --p-radius-lg, --p-shadow; padding:0 so the header/body/footer own spacing; max-width/height + body scroll keep a tall modal in the viewport) and a small conventional structure so boards get a consistent modal: .dialog-header (title + a quiet .dialog-close ✕), .dialog-body (scrollable), and .dialog-footer (top --p-border, right-aligned buttons — neutral by default, .primary = --p-accent/--p-accent-text). It also themes `dialog::backdrop` with --p-overlay + a blur: ::backdrop lives in the TOP LAYER (not a child of <dialog>), but modern Chromium makes it INHERIT from its originating element, so the <html>-level --p-* resolve on it — VERIFIED in both dark and light. Wrap the contents in a `<form method="dialog">` so a footer button's `value` lands in dialog.returnValue (read it on the `close` event). For a form that submits to a script, DON'T use method="dialog" — intercept submit, run persephone.execute(), and close() on success so a failed save keeps the modal open. See the demo board's app.js for the backdrop-click-to-close helper and the execute()-backed form.
